title: Semi-structured data and distributed SQL
summary: Compare relational, XML/JSON-like, and distributed SQL workflows by schema, nesting, validation, and movement costs.
objectives: Recognize XML and JSON as semi-structured representations
Relate a distributed SQL query to parsing, shuffle, and compute costs

sections.title: Nested structure, delayed agreement
sections.body: XML uses user-defined tags, while JSON represents nested objects and arrays through key–value pairs. Semi-structured formats preserve variation and nesting, but consumers must do more interpretation and validation later.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The lecture introduces semi-structured data as a model choice, not as a replacement for relational integrity in every workload.

sections.title: Distributed SQL is still semantic SQL
sections.body: A distributed query engine changes the physical cost model, not the need to define a clear result. Joins, grouping, and sorting can move data across partitions, so the plan should be inspected for shuffle, skew, and serialization.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: This is the bridge from the introductory database engine to later distributed data systems: the same query semantics meet a different execution environment.

examples.title: Choosing a representation
steps: Use a relational schema when stable identity and constraints dominate.
Use nested XML or JSON when variation and hierarchy are first-class.
Define validation rules at the boundary where consumers need them.
Measure parse and shuffle costs when the query runs across partitions.
examples.answer: Flexibility is not free: deferred schema decisions move work into query and validation stages.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which representation naturally expresses nested variation with user-defined tags or key–value objects?
contrastDrills.explanation: XML and JSON represent nested or variable structure more directly; they do not remove the need for validation.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the boundary between the two concepts before choosing.

contrastDrills.prompt: What is the main trade-off of schema-on-read?
choices: It delays some schema and validation work until query time
contrastDrills.explanation: Schema-on-read is flexible at ingestion but shifts interpretation and validation to downstream consumers.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the boundary between the two concepts before choosing.

math.explanation: Semi-structured and distributed workflows add costs beyond the logical query. Parsing nested records, moving rows across partitions, computing the transformation, and writing the result are separate places to measure.
math.name: Distributed scan cost decomposition
math.purpose: Use it to diagnose repeated scans, data movement, and synchronization in a large-data workflow.
math.caveat: This is an engineering decomposition, not an exact runtime law.

criticalQuestions.prompt: When is schema-on-read the wrong choice even if ingestion flexibility is attractive?
criticalQuestions.angle: Consider repeated consumers, strict governance, latency, and the cost of discovering errors late.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: If many consumers need the same stable semantics or correctness must be enforced at ingestion, a validated schema-on-write boundary may reduce duplicated downstream work.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why can a short SQL query still trigger an expensive distributed job?
criticalQuestions.angle: Trace partitioning, joins, shuffles, serialization, and synchronization rather than counting SQL tokens.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The logical query hides physical movement. A group-by or join can require a wide exchange even when the query text is only a few lines.
